milestones.title: Qin establishes Qiantang County
milestones.detail: After conquering the south-east the First Emperor of Qin set up Qiantang as a county under Kuaiji Commandery, near the Wulin hills west of the later city. It is the conventional documented beginning of the city; Yuhang, now one of Hangzhou's districts, appears in written records earlier.

milestones.title: Hang Prefecture created; first city wall built
milestones.detail: The Sui dynasty made the town the seat of Hang Prefecture (Hangzhou) in 589, which gave the city its name and entitled it to a city wall, built two years later.

milestones.title: Grand Canal reaches Hangzhou
milestones.detail: The Jiangnan Canal was completed about 609-610, linking Hangzhou north to Suzhou and Yangzhou and making the city the southern terminus of the Grand Canal.

milestones.title: Capital of the Wuyue kingdom
milestones.detail: With the fall of the Tang, Wuyue became independent with Hangzhou (then called Xifu) as its capital until 978. Its kings extended the walls and sea dykes and built the pagodas around West Lake.

milestones.title: Su Shi builds the Su Causeway
milestones.detail: The poet-governor Su Shi used 200,000 workers to dredge West Lake and build a 2.8 km causeway across it from the dredged mud.

milestones.title: Song court arrives; Lin'an becomes the capital
milestones.detail: After Kaifeng fell to the Jurchens, Emperor Gaozong reached Hangzhou in 1129, and it was chosen as the Southern Song capital in 1132 under the name Lin'an. It remained the capital until 1276.

milestones.title: Great fire burns 58,097 houses
milestones.detail: The worst of several Song-era fires burned for four days across a three-mile area. Other major fires struck in 1229, 1237 and 1275.
milestones.source: Gernet (1962), Daily Life in China on the Eve of the Mongol Invasion, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hangzhou#History

milestones.title: Mongol armies take the city
milestones.detail: Kublai Khan's forces captured Hangzhou three years before the final collapse of the Southern Song. The city was spared and remained the main commercial centre of the south under the Yuan.

milestones.title: Taiping siege and capture
milestones.detail: Taiping forces besieged Hangzhou from October and took it on 28 December 1861. Qing forces under Zuo Zongtang retook it on 31 March 1864, by when most of the population had died or fled.

milestones.title: Opened to foreign trade
milestones.detail: Hangzhou opened as a treaty port under the Treaty of Shimonoseki, and a Japanese concession was laid out.

milestones.title: Shanghai-Hangzhou railway completed
milestones.detail: The railway cut the journey from Shanghai from three days by boat to about three hours.

milestones.title: Manchu city walls demolished
milestones.detail: The walls of the Manchu district, including the section between the city and West Lake, were dismantled. From 1913 the area was sold off as the New Business District, opening the city to the lake.

milestones.title: Qiantang Bridge opens; Japanese occupation
milestones.detail: The Qiantang River Bridge was completed on 29 September 1937; in November its builders were ordered to prepare its demolition to slow the Japanese advance. The occupation of Hangzhou began on 23-24 December and lasted until 1945.

milestones.title: West Lake inscribed by UNESCO
milestones.detail: The West Lake Cultural Landscape of Hangzhou was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

milestones.title: Metro Line 1 opens
milestones.detail: Hangzhou Metro Line 1 opened on 24 November 2012, six years after construction began.

milestones.title: Hangzhou hosts the 19th Asian Games
milestones.detail: The 2022 Asian Games, postponed by a year, were held from 23 September to 8 October 2023. The 80,000-seat Olympic Sports Center stadium had been completed in 2018.

landmarks.name: Leifeng Pagoda (original)
landmarks.note: Height of about 50 m is inferred from Republican-era photographs of the ruined tower. It collapsed on 25 September 1924.

landmarks.name: Liuhe Pagoda (Six Harmonies Pagoda)
landmarks.note: First built in 970, destroyed in 1121 and rebuilt by 1165; the timber outer eaves are Ming-Qing additions.

landmarks.name: Gongchen Bridge
landmarks.note: First built in 1631 and rebuilt in 1885.

landmarks.name: Baochu Pagoda
landmarks.source: Zhejiang Provincial Cultural Heritage Bureau, via https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/保俶塔 ; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baochu_Pagoda
landmarks.note: First built in 963 with nine storeys. The present seven-storey tower dates from a Republican-era rebuilding, given as 1933 by English Wikipedia and 1924 by Chinese Wikipedia.

notes: Start date: 222 BCE, when the Qin set up Qiantang County, is the conventional documented beginning and is not contested, but the Qin county seat lay by the Wulin hills west of West Lake; the walled city on the present site dates from the Sui wall of 591. The Neolithic Liangzhu city (c. 3300-2300 BCE) in today's Yuhang District is a separate, earlier settlement and is not used as the start. Population: no estimate exists before 591, so the first eight centuries show no figure. All points are Chandler's (1987) estimates as digitised by Reba, Reitsma & Seto (2016); round-century and turning-point years were kept and Chandler's other years (622, 1077, 1170, 1201, 1360, 1450, 1550, 1575, 1625, 1650, 1657, 1681, 1731, 1825) dropped. The Southern Song peak is strongly contested: Chandler gives 255,000 (1200) and 432,000 (1273-1350), whereas Modelski and Morris give about 1,000,000 for 1200, Modelski 1,500,000 for 1300, Gernet 'well over one million' by 1276, and the Encyclopaedia Britannica over 2 million (all as quoted on Wikipedia's Hangzhou and 'List of largest cities throughout history' pages). The Chandler series was kept throughout for consistency of method; the true peak was very probably higher than shown. Wikipedia's Timeline of Hangzhou also quotes 1.75 million for 1275 (flagged there as dubious), 600,000 swelling to as much as 2.3 million with refugees in 1861, and a 1911 population of 141,859 (Gao 2004); none of these were verified against the original and they are not in the series. No pre-1950 Chinese census figure was located. Landmarks: the Mahavira Hall of Lingyin Temple (33.6 m), Chenghuang Pavilion (41.6 m), the Phoenix Mosque, the Qiantang River Bridge, the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception and the Olympic Sports Center stadium were left out because either the height or the completion year of the present structure could not be sourced. Modern tower heights, years and coordinates are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center city listing for Hangzhou (WGS-84). Monument coordinates are from Wikipedia.
